headline: Summoning both sides of the coal strike
summary: Roosevelt wires John Mitchell asking to see him on October 3 about the failing coal supply, and invites railroad chief Alexander Cassatt and Senator Quay into the effort. He also sends condolences to Isabella Craig, whose son William, a Secret Service agent, died in the Pittsfield crash. Edith gets her first look at the rebuilt White House and plans an upstairs office for herself.

headline: Smaller spurs and a mending leg

summary: Roosevelt holds more strike meetings with Root and Knox and sees Wilkins of the Washington Post. He writes Villard on whether sending soldiers to work the mines would be possible or lawful, and praises Silas McBee's strike column.

summary: On Kermit's 13th birthday, the Cabinet meets on the strike and Roosevelt receives the U.S. minister to Belgium. headline: A Siamese prince and more strike talks
summary: Roosevelt keeps up the strike meetings with his Cabinet, Wright and Sargent, sees Noyes of the Washington Star, and receives a prince of Siam. It is his niece Eleanor's 18th birthday. He praises Governor Odell's stand and answers John Kernan's request to serve on the commission.

headline: Up on crutches
summary: Strike meetings go on, with Root and Quay among the callers and Jenks at six. Cleveland agrees to serve on the commission. Roosevelt writes that he can now move about on crutches, and that while he is supposed to be minding Ethel, she will likely end up minding him.

headline: Morgan brings a plan to Jackson Place
summary: Roosevelt asks General Schofield about having the Army run the mines and receives the Chief Justice and the Supreme Court. That evening J. P. Morgan and Robert Bacon, fresh from talks with Root aboard Morgan's yacht Corsair, call on the President at his temporary quarters on Jackson Place. They agree to push the operators to accept a commission of Roosevelt's choosing, with the threat of Army control of the mines in the background.

headline: Settlement draws near
summary: Roosevelt confers with Wright and Wellman. He tells John Kernan the earlier commission plan must be dropped and writes Bishop that the strike is closer to ending. Back on Long Island, Sagamore Hill has Mrs. Clifford Richardson as a guest.

summary: Roosevelt names a seven-man commission to settle the coal strike: retired Army engineer General John M. Wilson; Labor Commissioner Carroll Wright; federal Judge George Gray of Delaware; E. E. Clark, head of the railway conductors' union, seated under the label of "eminent sociologist"; mining engineer Edward Parker; coal man Thomas Watkins; and Bishop John Spalding. He thanks Morgan and Hanna, explains to Cleveland that the operators would not accept him, and sends Mitchell the names.

headline: An order on political contributions

summary: Root, Hitchcock, Knox and Japanese minister Takahira call; Roosevelt lunches with Judge Gray and dines at Hay's. headline: The coal strike ends
summary: The anthracite strike is formally over. Roosevelt has John Kernan and M. E. Egan to lunch, and writes Taft that his Rome mission has failed and resentment of the Catholic church is growing in the Philippines.

summary: Roosevelt's essay "The Presidency" appears in Youth's Companion. headline: Moving into the rebuilt White House

summary: In New York Roosevelt meets Nicholas Murray Butler for breakfast at the University Club, speaks at the dedication of the Chamber of Commerce building, and argues for military preparedness at a dinner at the Waldorf-Astoria. At midnight he leaves on a hunting trip.

headline: Sunday callers Shaw and Spooner
summary: Treasury Secretary Shaw calls in the morning and Senator Spooner in the evening.

headline: Photographed, then back to work
summary: Mr. Ingersoll photographs Roosevelt in the morning. He confers with Hay and Cullom, goes over the Cuba treaty with Root, lunches with Sheffield, Boardman and Devereaux, and has a dinner at eight.

events.detail: Three lunch guests, among them James Sheffield

headline: Ships ordered toward the blockade
summary: After a Cabinet session on Cuba and Venezuela, Roosevelt decides to send American warships from Culebra into the blockade zone and hands reporters battle maps of the area. He works on the Militia Bill with Root, Proctor, Hull and Dick, and dines with a large party of congressional leaders.

events.detail: Orders U.S. ships from Culebra into the blockade area
Gives the press maps of the zone
Militia Bill with Root, Proctor, Hull and Dick
Dinner with Allison, Hanna, Cannon and others

headline: Tracey for the Philippine bench
summary: On a busy day Hanna, Dillingham, Tawney, Martin and Clarkson call, and Roosevelt has Joseph Barnes, Stranahan and Clarkson to lunch. He tells James Tracey he wants him on the Philippine Supreme Court.

events.detail: Lunch with Clarkson, Stranahan and Barnes

letters.topic: Wishes to name him to the Philippine high court

headline: Britain asks Roosevelt to arbitrate
summary: Britain agrees the Venezuela dispute should be arbitrated and asks Roosevelt to serve as arbiter. Roosevelt later said he warned Germany of war if it refused arbitration. The Pacific fleet begins maneuvers, alarming German envoy Holleben. The day ends with the annual Cabinet dinner.

events.detail: Britain accepts arbitration and invites Roosevelt to arbitrate

references.title: The Letters of Theodore Roosevelt (Morison), letter to William Roscoe Thayer, August 21, 1916

uncertain: Roosevelt's claim of a war threat to Germany comes from his later recollection, not a contemporary record.

headline: Germany agrees to arbitrate
summary: Germany agrees to arbitration over Venezuela. The Cabinet meets on the crisis, and Roosevelt discusses currency with Lyman Gage and J. H. Rhoades.

events.detail: Germany accepts arbitration of the Venezuela dispute

headline: Mrs. Grant's funeral; off to the Rapidan
summary: Roosevelt breakfasts with Jacob Riis. Congress adjourns, Julia Dent Grant is buried, and after a meeting with Hay Roosevelt leaves for Rapidan, Virginia.

headline: Guest of Joseph Wilmer
summary: At Rapidan, Virginia, Roosevelt stays with Joseph Wilmer.

headline: Coal tariffs
summary: Back in Washington, Roosevelt meets Hay and writes Henry Higginson about duties on coal.

letters.topic: Tariffs on coal

headline: Mabini in a Philippine jail
summary: After a Cabinet meeting on Venezuela and lunch with George Perkins, Roosevelt writes Senator Hoar about Apolinario Mabini, the insurgent leader held by the United States in the Philippines.

letters.topic: The imprisoned Filipino leader Mabini

headline: Christmas Eve with Hay and the Sun
summary: Roosevelt confers with Hay on Venezuela, sees a Sun newspaperman named Matthews, and asks William Allen White whether Leonard Wood can stay at his club.

events.detail: Meeting with Matthews of the Sun
Writes White about lodging for Wood

letters.topic: Could Wood stay at White's club?

headline: Christmas at the White House
summary: The children are banging on the bedroom door by 6:45, and soon they are piled on the bed opening stockings; Archie has hidden a small gift-laden tree in a closet. After breakfast Archie gets a rifle and riding boots and Quentin an electric train. Roosevelt rides for three hours, lunches at Bamie's, fences single-stick with Wood and Ferguson, and ends with dinner and dancing in the East Room.

events.detail: Stockings opened on the bed at dawn
Gifts in the library; Archie rides Algonquin
Three-hour ride with Ted, Ferguson and Wood
Christmas dinner and East Room dance

headline: Venezuela headed to The Hague
summary: After a Cabinet meeting, the government announces the Venezuela dispute will go to the Hague Tribunal. Roosevelt sends a Christmas letter to young James A. Garfield, and writes Shaw, Taft and Cleveland about upholding the Monroe Doctrine, Agassiz on the Philippines and Schurz on the arbitration.

Letters to young Garfield, Shaw, Taft, Cleveland, Agassiz, Schurz and Perkins

headline: The Austrian ambassador calls
summary: Roosevelt receives the Austrian ambassador in the morning and writes Root and the Rev. William Rainsford, the latter on the trusts.

headline: Got what he wanted on Venezuela
summary: Wilson and Foulke call, Roosevelt lunches with psychologist Hugo Münsterberg, and Justice White visits in the evening. He writes George Hinman that he knew his aims in the Venezuela settlement and achieved them.

letters.topic: Achieved exactly his goals in Venezuela

headline: Land Office business
summary: The Cabinet meets on General Land Office affairs. Roosevelt meets a Picayune editor, Mr. Robertson, and confers with Generals Young and Wood.
